Reconcile span line-range drift and doc citations after rebasing onto main

Rebasing cards/main-168/1 onto main's advanced tip (which had picked up substantial,
unrelated rename-collapse and mid-rebase-labeling work touching the same cli/mod.rs
region this card's commits also shifted) produced textual conflicts in every .span/
anchor file and wiki doc citation that pins a line range inside cli/mod.rs's Cli
struct, Commands enum, and dispatch function. Each side's line numbers were stale in
a different way, so conflicts were resolved provisionally by keeping one side, then
verified and corrected properly against the actual post-rebase file via `git span
stale --fix` (which reconciled five spans' worth of pure line-shift drift with zero
content change) and a manual edit to wiki/meta/git-span-documentation-touchpoints.md's
two mod.rs citation links, which `git span stale` cannot catch on its own since it
verifies the doc paragraph's own content hash, not the accuracy of line numbers
quoted inside that prose.

The `.wiki/` mirror root's own copy of this coupling is a separate system owned by
the `wiki` extension binary, not `git-span` — that binary was unavailable this
session (spawn timeout), and its own pre-commit hook is explicitly best-effort
(`command -v wiki >/dev/null 2>&1 || exit 0`, never blocks a commit), so it is left
for that tool to reconcile once available rather than hand-edited against an
unfamiliar format.

`git span stale` now reports 0 stale across 45 spans, and a full `yarn validate` at
the workspace root passes clean.
EOF
)" && git log --oneline -1

EOF

command:
cd $WORKSPACE_PATH && git add -A && git commit -q -F - <<'COMMITMSG'
Add the stale-to-drift rename script, dry run only

`scripts/rename-stale-to-drift.sh` mechanizes the retirement of "stale" as git-span's word for an anchor's drift status. This commit adds the script and its dry run; it does not apply the rename.

git-span has said the same thing two ways for a while. The type system and label formatter call it drift — [DriftSource](./packages/git-span/src/types.rs#L450), [format_drift_label](./packages/git-span/src/cli/drift_label.rs) — while the subcommand, the tests, the VS Code span viewer, and most of the docs call it stale. Every explanation of the concept has had to translate between the two first. Doing this by hand was never realistic: the term appears across 199 files in the allowlist alone, and a repo-wide grep returns roughly 1,700 hits of which the large majority belong to something else entirely.

The script is modelled on [rebrand-mesh-to-span.sh](./scripts/rebrand-mesh-to-span.sh), which did this same job for `git mesh` to `git span` and had already worked out the shape: dry run by default, `--diff` to review, `--apply` to write, and curated phrase rules that assert an exact match count so a rule that stops matching fails loudly instead of quietly under-applying. The decisive design choice is that it works from an explicit path **allowlist** rather than a denylist. With this hit ratio a denylist doesn't fail visibly, it just grows a hole — and the thing a hole lets through is a doc still telling an agent to run `git span stale`, which breaks nothing until an agent actually tries it.

The interesting work turned out to be deciding what *isn't* in scope, and the useful test was whether a sentence would still be true in a tool that had no concept of anchors. Ordinary cache and build staleness inside `packages/git-span` passes that test and stays: a stale lock file, a stale digest, `prune stale sessions`, and [cleanup-stale-target.sh](./packages/git-sp...

command:
cd $WORKSPACE_PATH && git add -A && git commit -q -F - <<'EOF'
Retire the addresses the rebase left behind, and finish the merge it could not

Rebasing this branch onto main replayed thirteen commits, and the declarations came out the other side describing a repository that does not exist. Twenty-five anchors read drifted, one span carried three records for a single identity, and twenty-nine mesh anchors pointed at windows whose hashes match no content in any tree. None of it was upstream drift. All of it was manufactured here.

The mechanism is worth stating plainly, because it is the same defect this card was opened to repair, turned against the card's own branch. `git span add` writes a record at the address it is given and retires nothing. Every replayed commit that re-anchored a span therefore deposited one more address for a region that already had one, and because those addresses differ by a line or two they are distinct identities — which is precisely the state the collapse sweep cannot see. The sweep keys on `(path, start_line, end_line)`; N stale addresses for one region are N identities, and it correctly declines to touch them. `--fix` ran cleanly over this tree and reduced nothing, exactly as designed. The feature is not at fault; its boundary is just narrower than the damage.

The tempting repair was to restore `.span/` from main and re-anchor once. It would have produced a green tree in a minute, and it would have been wrong: `conflict-residue-boundary` holds a relationship main has no record of, introduced deliberately on this branch, and a wholesale restore would have deleted it silently. So each cluster was settled on evidence instead. Where a record carried main's pre-edit hash while a fresh successor already sat at the shifted address, the predecessor was residue and was retired. Collapse the mesh records this branch duplicated, and re-anchor what the commit hook moved

That one is re-anchored in place here: same address, changed content, no boundary moved.

The larger problem was quieter. Across the twenty mesh files this branch touched, duplicate records had grown from eight groups to twenty. Three channels, all silent, in the same shape this card has been documenting all along — the report is accurate about what it measures and useless for what you wanted to know.

The repair had a false start worth recording. `wiki mesh add` is documented as an upsert, so the obvious move was to add each duplicated anchor and let the upsert collapse it. What works is `remove` followed by `add` — remove drops every copy at an address, add writes one back and re-hashes it from current bytes.

## Independent evidence for the principle, from another subsystem

While this card was in flight, an unrelated repair produced a clean witness for
the same design argument, which is worth recording because it arrived from
outside the span reader entirely.

Commit `6cced803` added seven lines of doc comment to
[`cli/mod.rs`](packages/git-span/src/cli/mod.rs) and re-anchored the declarations
whose *addresses* those lines moved, while missing every declaration whose
*bytes* they changed. That left twelve stale anchors across seven `.wiki/`
meshes. Eleven of them were ordinary hash staleness: silent, invisible to the
commit hook unless it happened to touch that mesh, and individually harmless.

The twelfth was different. `wiki/guides/cache-path-counters` was anchored at
`#L101-L184` of a file that had held 183 lines since `e1b64add` shrank it, and
`wiki mesh add` **refused it outright** — "out of bounds: file has 183 line(s)" —
rather than re-hashing whatever was there. That refusal is what prompted a sweep
of every mesh in the repository, which is how the other eleven were found.

The parallel to `resolve` is exact. A tool that fails closed on the one input it
cannot verify produced the only signal that made eleven silent failures
findable; a tool that had guessed would have re-hashed the moved extent, gone
green, and left all twelve wrong. That is the same trade this document argues
for at the anchor/why boundary — refusing a small set of inputs the reader
cannot establish, in exchange for never silently writing a coupling nobody
declared. Here the trade paid out in a subsystem that knows nothing about
conflict residue, which is the strongest kind of evidence for a design
principle: it was not built to demonstrate it.
EOF
